summary: Defines conventions for using Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) algorithms, including quantum-secure ones, in the Cryptographic Message Syntax to encrypt and decrypt content. It updates RFC 5652.

plainLanguage.summary:
CMS is the container format used for signed and encrypted email and for many other signed or encrypted data. It has ways to share the content key, but not one that fits the newer key encapsulation algorithms, including the ones designed to resist a quantum computer.

RFC 9629 adds that way. A new record in the message carries the encapsulated key, and a key derivation function turns the shared secret it produces into a key that encrypts the content key for that recipient.

questions: what is a kem in cms
how does cms use post-quantum kems
subtitle: How CMS messages can be encrypted with key encapsulation mechanisms, including quantum-secure ones.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax supports key transport and key agreement for sharing the content-encryption key, but newer Key Encapsulation Mechanism algorithms, including quantum-secure ones, had no defined way to be used.
tldr.mechanism: A new recipient-information type, KEMRecipientInfo, carries the KEM ciphertext. A key derivation function turns the KEM shared secret into a key-encryption key, which then encrypts the content-encryption key for that recipient.
tldr.outcome: CMS enveloped-data, authenticated-data and authenticated-enveloped-data messages can now use any KEM that meets the security requirements. The RFC updates RFC 5652.

today: RFC 9629 was published in August 2024 and is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 5652 by adding KEM support to CMS.

sections.title: Why CMS Needs KEMs
sections.content:
This document updates the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) of RFC 5652. The CMS enveloped-data content type and the CMS authenticated-enveloped-data content type of RFC 5083 support both key transport and key agreement algorithms to establish the key used to encrypt and decrypt the content. Cryptographers have more recently been specifying Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) algorithms, including quantum-secure ones, and this document defines conventions for using them.

A KEM is a one-pass, store-and-forward mechanism for transporting random keying material to a recipient using the recipient's public key. The originator and the recipient do not need to be online at the same time. The recipient's private key recovers the random keying material, which is then treated as a pairwise shared secret between the two.

The KEM algorithm provides three functions. KeyGen() produces a public key and a private key. Encapsulate(pk) produces a ciphertext for the recipient and a shared secret for the originator. Decapsulate(sk, ct) produces the shared secret for the recipient. To support a particular KEM algorithm, the CMS originator MUST implement Encapsulate, and the CMS recipient MUST implement KeyGen and Decapsulate. The recipient's public key is usually carried in a certificate.

Security in this setting depends on three things: the KEM must be secure against adaptive chosen ciphertext attacks; the key-encryption algorithm must provide both confidentiality and integrity; and the choices of the key derivation function and the key-encryption algorithm must give the same level of security as the KEM.
sections.plainLanguage: A KEM lets one party send random keying material to another using only the second party's public key, without either of them having to be online at the same time. The sender wraps the material, the receiver unwraps it with its private key, and both end up with the same shared secret.

sections.title: How the Key Reaches the Recipient
sections.content:
KEM algorithms can be used with three CMS content types: enveloped-data, authenticated-data and authenticated-enveloped-data. The overview uses the terminology of enveloped-data.

The originator generates the content-encryption key (or the content-authenticated-encryption key) at random, and every recipient obtains that same key as an encrypted object inside the encryptedKey field of the KEMRecipientInfo. All recipients then use it to decrypt the message.

For each recipient, the originator uses the recipient's public key with the KEM Encapsulate function to get a pairwise shared secret and a ciphertext for that recipient. A key derivation function turns that shared secret into a pairwise key-encryption key, and that key encrypts the content key for this recipient only. The content key itself then encrypts the content for everyone.

The recipient does the mirror image. Its private key and the ciphertext give the pairwise shared secret, the key derivation function gives the key-encryption key, that key decrypts the content key, and the content key decrypts the content.

In advance, each recipient uses the KEM KeyGen function to create a key pair and usually obtains a certificate that includes the new public key. Whether or not the public key is certified, it has to be made available to potential originators.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender picks one content key for the whole message. For each recipient it derives a separate wrapping key from a shared secret, and uses that to encrypt the content key. The recipient unwraps in the reverse order and ends up with the same content key as everyone else.

sections.title: The KEMRecipientInfo Structure
sections.content:
Recipient information for additional key management techniques is represented in the OtherRecipientInfo type of RFC 5652, and each technique is identified by a unique ASN.1 object identifier. The identifier for KEMRecipientInfo is id-ori-kem, which is id-ori 3.

The structure has eight fields. version is the syntax version number and MUST be 0. rid specifies the recipient's certificate or key used with the Encapsulate function, either by the issuer's distinguished name and serial number or by a key identifier; implementations MUST support both alternatives for recipient processing and at least one for originator processing. The certificate MUST contain a KEM public key, and an X.509 version 3 certificate with a key usage extension MUST assert the keyEncipherment bit. kem identifies the KEM algorithm and its parameters. kemct is the ciphertext produced by Encapsulate for this recipient. kdf identifies the key derivation function. kekLength is the size of the key-encryption key in octets, an integer from 1 to 65535, which is one of the inputs to the key derivation function. ukm is optional user keying material used as context input. wrap identifies the key-encryption algorithm, and encryptedKey is the result of encrypting the content key with the key-encryption key.
sections.plainLanguage: The new record names the recipient's certificate, the KEM algorithm, the ciphertext the KEM produced, the key derivation function, the length of the wrapping key, the wrapping algorithm, and the wrapped content key itself. The version number is fixed at zero.

sections.title: Deriving the Key-Encryption Key
sections.content:
The key derivation function takes three inputs. IKM is the input keying material, a symmetric secret, which in this case is the shared secret the KEM produced; the algorithm used to derive it depends on the KEM. L is the length of the output keying material in octets, taken from the kekLength field, whose value depends on the key-encryption algorithm. info is contextual input, and is the DER-encoded CMSORIforKEMOtherInfo structure, which holds the key-encryption algorithm identifier, the kekLength, and the optional user keying material.

The output is the output keying material, exactly L octets long, and that is the key-encryption key used to encrypt the content key.

An acceptable key derivation function MUST accept IKM, L and info as inputs, and MAY also accept a salt value carried as a parameter to the key derivation algorithm identifier. All of these inputs MUST influence the output.
sections.plainLanguage: The wrapping key is not the shared secret itself. It is computed from the shared secret, a length, and a description of what the wrapping key will be used for. That last input ties the key to this particular message and recipient.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5652 apply. Beyond them, the KEM algorithm MUST be designed to be secure when the public key is used many times. A KEM with a single-use public key is not appropriate, because the public key is expected to sit in a long-lived certificate and be used over and over, so algorithms offering indistinguishability under adaptive chosen ciphertext attack are appropriate. A common design pattern for that is the Fujisaki-Okamoto transform or a variant of it.

The key derivation function SHOULD offer at least the security level of the KEM, and so should the key-encryption algorithm and the size of the key-encryption key.

KEM algorithms do not provide data origin authentication, so when a KEM is used with the authenticated-data content type, the contents are delivered with integrity from an unknown source.

Implementations MUST protect the KEM private key, the key-encryption key and the content key. Compromise of the private key may disclose everything protected with it, whereas compromise of the wrapping key or the content key affects a single message. The shared secret and any random value the KEM used MUST NOT be reused for any other purpose, and both the originator and the recipient MUST discard the shared secret once the entry has been constructed.

Content keys and key pairs MUST be generated randomly, and RFC 4086 gives guidance on generating good random numbers. Where the key-encryption algorithm and the content-encryption algorithm use different key sizes, the effective security is the weaker of the two. The RFC closes by noting that cryptographic algorithms weaken over time, so implementations should be modular enough to take on new algorithms later.
sections.plainLanguage: The KEM has to be safe to use with the same public key again and again, which rules out algorithms designed for one use only. The wrapping key and the content key must be generated at random and kept secret, and the shared secret must be thrown away once it has been used.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: For the KEMRecipientInfo defined in Section 3, IANA has assigned an object identifier in the "SMI Security for S/MIME Other Recipient Info Identifiers" registry, whose base is 1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.13. The value id-ori-kem is id-ori 3. The document also provides two ASN.1 modules: one extending the AlgorithmInformation-2009 module to define the KEM-ALGORITHM class, and one defining the structures needed to use KEM algorithms with CMS. The first module uses EXPLICIT tagging and the second IMPLICIT tagging, and both follow the conventions of RFC 5911, RFC 5912 and RFC 6268.
sections.plainLanguage: The new record type gets a registered object identifier, and the RFC publishes the ASN.1 modules that describe it so that implementations can agree on the exact encoding.

messages.label: Encapsulate(recipient pk)
messages.note: Produces the shared secret and the ciphertext for this recipient.

messages.note: The key derivation function turns the shared secret into a wrapping key.

messages.note: The wrapping key encrypts the content key for this recipient.

messages.note: The private key gives the shared secret, the wrapping key gives the content key.

data.title: KEMRecipientInfo
data.code:
KEMRecipientInfo ::= SEQUENCE {
  version CMSVersion,  -- always set to 0
  rid RecipientIdentifier,
  kem KEMAlgorithmIdentifier,
  kemct OCTET STRING,
  kdf KeyDerivationAlgorithmIdentifier,
  kekLength INTEGER (1..65535),
  ukm [0] EXPLICIT UserKeyingMaterial OPTIONAL,
  wrap KeyEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier,
  encryptedKey EncryptedKey }

viz.caption: WHAT THE RFC REQUIRES OF AN IMPLEMENTATION

items.title: Reusable public keys
items.text: The KEM must be secure when the same public key is used many times.

items.title: Fresh shared secrets
items.text: A new shared secret per recipient, and it must be discarded after use.

items.title: Protected keys
items.text: The KEM private key, the wrapping key and the content key must all be protected.

items.title: Random generation
items.text: Content keys and key pairs must come from a good random number generator.

items.title: The weakest link counts
items.text: Where the cipher sizes differ, the effective security is that of the weaker one.

items.title: Algorithms expire
items.text: Implementations should be modular so that new algorithms can be added later.
